missions/london-missionary-society/name: London Missionary Society (1795: Tahiti, Madagascar, Moffat, Livingstone)
missions/london-missionary-society/origi: London (Spa Fields and the Castle and Falcon, Aldersgate)
missions/london-missionary-society/statu: In 1966 the LMS merged with the Commonwealth Missionary Society to form the Congregational Council for World Mission, and in 1977 it was restructured as the Council for World Mission (CWM), a partnership of about 30 member churches, most of them former LMS fields in the Pacific, Africa, India and East Asia, which share resources and decision-making as equals.
missions/london-missionary-society/summa: Founded in 1795 as 'the Missionary Society' by evangelical Congregationalists, Anglicans, Presbyterians and Methodists, the LMS aimed to send 'not Presbyterianism, Independency, Episcopacy, or any other form of church government', but 'the glorious Gospel of the blessed God'. Its ship Duff carried thirty missionaries to Tahiti in 1796–97, beginning Protestant Christianity in Polynesia; it went on to plant churches in South Africa, Madagascar, India, China, Siberia, Guyana and New Guinea, through figures such as John Williams, Robert Moffat, David Livingstone, Robert Morrison and James Chalmers, and through hundreds of Pacific Islander and African evangelists.
missions/london-missionary-society/story:
Stirred by Carey's letters from Bengal and by the evangelical revival, ministers including David Bogue of Gosport, the Anglican Thomas Haweis and John Eyre met from 1794 and founded the Missionary Society in London on 22 September 1795. Its 'Fundamental Principle' (1796) declared that the society would send the gospel without any particular form of church order, leaving converts to choose their own; in practice, as Anglicans and Presbyterians formed their own societies, the LMS became chiefly Congregationalist. It was renamed the London Missionary Society in 1818.

The first venture was dramatic. The society bought the ship Duff and, under Captain James Wilson, sent thirty missionaries, only four of them ordained (the rest artisans such as carpenters, weavers, a bricklayer and a surgeon), some accompanied by wives and children. Leaving the Thames on 10 August 1796 and Portsmouth in September, the Duff called at Rio de Janeiro, rounded the Cape of Good Hope and crossed the Southern Ocean to Tahiti, anchoring in Matavai Bay on 5 March 1797. Eighteen missionaries landed there; others were left on Tongatapu and on Tahuata in the Marquesas before the ship returned via Canton. The Tonga and Marquesas missions failed within a few years, and most of the Tahiti party fled to New South Wales in 1798. A remnant led by Henry Nott persisted, and in 1812 the chief Pomare II asked for baptism; after his victory at Fei Pi in 1815 Tahiti rapidly became Christian, and the missionaries helped draft the Pomare Code of 1819. Nott completed the Tahitian Bible in 1835.

From Tahiti and the Society Islands, John Williams turned the mission outward. With Raiatean and Tahitian teachers such as Papeiha, who landed on Aitutaki in 1821 and Rarotonga in 1823, he spread Christianity to the Cook Islands, sailed his own ship, the Messenger of Peace, to Samoa in 1830, and was killed on landing at Dillon's Bay on Erromango in the New Hebrides on 20 November 1839. Pacific Islander teachers, many of whom also died, carried the faith on to Niue, Tuvalu, the Loyalty Islands and, from 1871, to Papua, where W. G. Lawes settled at Port Moresby in 1874 and James Chalmers was killed on Goaribari Island in 1901.

In South Africa the Dutch physician Johannes van der Kemp began work among the Khoikhoi in 1799 and founded Bethelsdorp in 1803; his successor as superintendent, John Philip, published Researches in South Africa (1828), which helped secure Ordinance 50 (1828) granting the Khoikhoi legal rights, and made him hated by settlers. Robert and Mary Moffat founded Kuruman in 1824 among the Tlhaping (Tswana), where Moffat printed the complete Setswana Bible in 1857. Their daughter Mary married David Livingstone, who arrived in 1841 and moved north to Mabotsa and Kolobeng; with few converts, he turned to exploration, crossing the Kalahari to Lake Ngami (1849), reaching the Zambezi (1851), crossing Africa from Luanda to Quelimane (1853–56) and publicising the East African slave trade. He resigned from the LMS in 1857, but his call for 'Christianity and commerce' shaped Victorian mission and empire for decades. Further north the LMS entered Matabeleland at Inyati (1859) and Lake Tanganyika (1877).

In Madagascar the Welsh missionaries David Jones and Thomas Bevan arrived in 1818; under King Radama I the mission opened schools and printed the Malagasy Bible (1835) in the Latin script. Queen Ranavalona I then banned Christianity (1835), and during a quarter-century of persecution many Christians were killed, among them Rasalama (1837), while the church grew underground. Ranavalona II was baptised in 1869 and ordered the burning of the royal sampy (talismans), making Protestant Christianity the religion of the Merina state, before French conquest in 1895–96. In Asia, Robert Morrison reached Canton in 1807 as the first Protestant missionary to China, completing a Chinese Bible with William Milne by 1823; the Anglo-Chinese College at Malacca, James Legge's translations of the Chinese Classics and Griffith John's work in Hankow followed. In South India Ringeltaube (from 1806) began the Travancore mission, whose churches grew among Nadars and Dalits; in Siberia Edward Stallybrass and William Swan translated the Bible into Mongolian among the Buryats (1817–40); and in Demerara (Guyana) the missionary John Smith died in prison in 1824 after being blamed for the 1823 slave rising.

The twentieth century brought devolution. LMS churches in South India joined the Church of South India in 1947, Chinese congregations entered the Church of Christ in China (1927) and later the post-1949 Three-Self structures, the Malagasy churches formed the FJKM in 1968, and Pacific churches became the Congregational Christian Church of Samoa, Ekalesia Kelisiano Tuvalu and others. In 1977 the LMS turned itself into the Council for World Mission, in which the former 'mission fields' are equal partners with the British churches.
missions/london-missionary-society/belie: Evangelical, broadly Calvinist Protestantism centred on the atoning death of Christ, the need for conversion and the authority of Scripture.
The 'Fundamental Principle' (1796): mission should spread the gospel, not a denominational form of church government, leaving converts to decide their church order.
Congregational polity in practice: self-governing local churches of professing believers.
A belief, shared by most missionaries, that Christianity, literacy, commerce and 'civilisation' went together, articulated most famously by Livingstone.
Anti-slavery conviction: many LMS missionaries opposed the slave trade and advocated for the rights of Khoikhoi, enslaved Africans and Pacific Islanders.
Postmillennial optimism that the gospel would steadily spread to all nations.
missions/london-missionary-society/strat: Sending artisan missionaries to model 'civilised' Christian life, as on the Duff in 1796.
Bible translation and printing: Tahitian, Rarotongan, Samoan, Setswana, Malagasy, Chinese, Mongolian and many other languages.
Use of Pacific Islander and African teachers and evangelists as the main agents of expansion, with European missionaries as supervisors.
Mission ships (the Duff, Camden, Messenger of Peace and a series of John Williams ships) linking scattered island stations.
Education, from village schools to colleges such as the Anglo-Chinese College (Malacca, 1818), Malua Theological College in Samoa (1844) and Tiger Kloof in South Africa (1904).
Political advocacy on behalf of indigenous peoples, as in John Philip's campaign at the Cape.
Medical missions, notably in China and India.
missions/london-missionary-society/group: Tahitians and Society Islanders, Cook Islanders, Samoans, Niueans, Tuvaluans, Loyalty Islanders and peoples of Papua.
Khoikhoi, Griqua, Tswana, Ndebele and Xhosa peoples of Southern Africa.
Merina and other peoples of Madagascar.
Cantonese and other Chinese communities in Southeast Asia and China.
Nadars and Dalit communities (Pulayas, Parayas) of South Travancore in India, and Telugu and Kannada speakers in Andhra and Karnataka.
Buryat Mongols in Siberia, Mongols in Inner Mongolia, and enslaved Africans in Demerara and Berbice (Guyana).
missions/london-missionary-society/chall: Early failures: the Duff missionaries largely abandoned Tahiti in 1798, and the Tonga and Marquesas missions collapsed.
Violence: missionaries and Islander teachers were killed in the New Hebrides and Papua, and Christians were persecuted in Madagascar (1835–61).
Disease and isolation, especially in central Africa and the Pacific.
Settler and planter hostility in the Cape Colony and Demerara toward missionary advocacy for indigenous and enslaved people.
Competition with Catholic, Anglican and other missions, as with French Catholic missions in Tahiti and Anglican missions in Madagascar.
Political upheaval in China (Taiping war, Boxer rising, the 1949 revolution), which ended LMS work there.
missions/london-missionary-society/harms: Missionary partisanship in Pacific politics: support for Pomare II's war of 1815 and the Pomare Code of 1819, which imposed missionary moral law with penalties.
Destruction of religious objects and sacred sites in Tahiti, Rarotonga and Madagascar (the burning of the sampy in 1869), and suppression of dance, tattooing and other customs.

In 1888 the LMS missionary Charles Helm witnessed and interpreted the Rudd Concession, misleading Lobengula about its terms, and John Smith Moffat (a former LMS missionary) negotiated the Moffat Treaty, both preparing for Rhodes's seizure of Matabeleland.
The Madagascar mission's identification with the Merina monarchy made Protestantism a state religion that subject peoples experienced as Merina domination.
George Pritchard's role as both missionary and British consul in Tahiti entangled the mission in the Anglo-French crisis of 1843–44 and the expulsion of Catholic priests in 1836.
Paternalism toward Islander teachers, who bore the greatest risks but received little recognition or authority until late in the mission's history.
missions/london-missionary-society/devel: Founded the Protestant churches of Polynesia, which remain central to national life in Samoa, Tuvalu, the Cook Islands, Niue and French Polynesia.
Translations of the Bible into Tahitian, Setswana, Malagasy, Chinese, Mongolian and many Pacific languages, with grammars and dictionaries.
Advocacy for indigenous rights, from Ordinance 50 at the Cape (1828) to campaigns against slavery and blackbirding.
Morrison's and Legge's sinology, which shaped Western understanding of Chinese language and classics.
Schools and colleges that educated generations of African, Malagasy, Indian and Pacific leaders.
The Council for World Mission (1977), a pioneering model of mission partnership among equals.
missions/london-missionary-society/outco: The LMS was one of the most influential Protestant missions of the nineteenth century, creating whole national churches in the South Pacific and Madagascar and significant ones in South Africa, India and China. Having become largely Congregationalist despite its non-denominational founding principle, it reconstituted itself in 1977 as the Council for World Mission, owned jointly by the churches it had helped to found.

missions/london-missionary-society/count: French Polynesia (Tahiti and the Society Islands)
Duff missionaries at Matavai Bay; Pomare II's conversion (1812) and the Tahitian Bible (1835). Work passed to the Paris Mission after French annexation.
Cook Islands
Raiatean teachers Papeiha and Vahapata, then Williams and Aaron Buzacott; the Cook Islands Christian Church.
Samoa
Williams and Tahitian teachers landed at Sapapali'i; Malua College (1844) trained Samoan pastors who served across the Pacific.
South Africa and Botswana
Bethelsdorp, Philip's advocacy, Moffat's Kuruman and Livingstone's stations at Mabotsa and Kolobeng.
Madagascar
Schools and translation under Radama I, persecution under Ranavalona I, and the conversion of the Merina monarchy in 1869.
China
Morrison at Canton and Macau, then Hong Kong, Shanghai, Hankow and Beijing; churches joined the Church of Christ in China (1927).
Malaysia and Singapore (Malacca)
William Milne's press and the Anglo-Chinese College (1818) served the Chinese diaspora before China opened.
India
Missions in Travancore (Nagercoil, Neyyoor), Bellary, Cuddapah, Vizagapatam and Bengal; South Indian churches joined the CSI in 1947.
Guyana (Demerara and Berbice)
John Wray and John Smith among enslaved Africans; Smith's death in prison (1824) fed British abolitionism.
Russia (Siberia, Buryatia)
Stallybrass and Swan translated the Bible into literary Mongolian until Nicholas I closed the mission in 1840.
Zimbabwe (Matabeleland)
Inyati mission among the Ndebele; LMS missionaries were drawn into the concessions that preceded colonisation.
Papua New Guinea
Loyalty Islander and Samoan teachers, Lawes at Port Moresby (1874) and Chalmers along the coast; today the United Church in Papua New Guinea.
Zambia and Tanzania (Lake Tanganyika)
Central African mission at Ujiji and later Mbereshi and Kawimbe, with heavy losses to disease.
Tuvalu, Niue and Kiribati
Samoan and other Islander pastors founded churches that became national churches.
missions/london-missionary-society/journ: The voyage of the Duff to Tahiti, Tonga and the Marquesas (1796–1798)
Captain James Wilson and thirty LMS missionaries, including Henry Nott and John Jefferson

The Duff left the Thames on 10 August 1796 and, after calling at Rio de Janeiro, went east round the Cape of Good Hope and south of Australia to reach Matavai Bay on 5 March 1797, where eighteen missionaries landed. Ten were left on Tongatapu and two on Tahuata; the ship returned to Tahiti and then sailed home by way of Canton, reaching England in July 1798.
John Williams, Mary Williams and Islander teachers including Papeiha

Based at Raiatea, Williams placed Islander teachers on Aitutaki and Rarotonga, built the Messenger of Peace on Rarotonga in 1827, and landed Tahitian teachers in Samoa in 1830. Returning to the Pacific after a celebrated tour of Britain, he was clubbed to death with James Harris on Erromango on 20 November 1839.
Robert Morrison's voyage to China via New York (1807)

Refused passage by the East India Company, Morrison sailed in January 1807 to New York and then on the American ship Trident to Macau and Canton, arriving in September 1807, where he lived precariously as an American-protected foreigner while learning Chinese.
Livingstone's early journeys from Kuruman to the Zambezi (1841–1851)
David Livingstone, with William Cotton Oswell and Mary Livingstone

From Moffat's Kuruman, Livingstone moved north to Mabotsa, where a lion mauled him, and to Kolobeng among the Kwena of Sechele, his only baptised convert. With Oswell he crossed the Kalahari to Lake Ngami in 1849 and reached the upper Zambezi in 1851.
Livingstone's crossing of Africa from Luanda to Quelimane (1853–1856)

Seeking a healthy route into the interior for missions and 'legitimate commerce', Livingstone travelled with Kololo companions from Linyanti to the Atlantic at Luanda (May 1854), returned, and followed the Zambezi to the Indian Ocean, becoming the first European known to have seen Victoria Falls (November 1855). His Missionary Travels (1857) made him a national hero.
Livingstone's last journey (1866–1873, after leaving the LMS)
David Livingstone with Susi, Chuma, Jacob Wainwright and others

Searching for the Nile's sources, Livingstone witnessed the massacre of hundreds of Manyema people at the Nyangwe market by slave-traders' gunmen (July 1871), met H. M. Stanley at Ujiji, and died at Chitambo's village on 1 May 1873. Susi and Chuma carried his body some 1,500 km to the coast, and his burial in Westminster Abbey (1874) spurred new Scottish and Anglican missions to central Africa.

The two Welsh missionaries landed at Tamatave in 1818; fever killed Bevan and both families and nearly killed Jones, who recovered in Mauritius and in 1820 was welcomed by Radama I at Antananarivo, opening the first schools.
missions/london-missionary-society/relat: The LMS's reliance on Tahitian, Rarotongan, Samoan and Loyalty Islander teachers created the Pacific Islander missionary movement.
Livingstone's death in 1873 prompted the Free Church of Scotland's Livingstonia (1875) and the Church of Scotland's Blantyre mission (1876).
The LMS and the American Board divided Pacific fields by comity and cooperated in Micronesia, Hawaii and China.
LMS leaders were active at Edinburgh 1910 and in the International Missionary Council, and the society's transformation into the Council for World Mission (1977) embodied ecumenical partnership.
missions/london-missionary-society/agree: Shared evangelical Calvinism, the voluntary-society model and priority on translation and education.
Many LMS missionaries (Moffat, Livingstone, Philip, Chalmers) were Scots, and the two shared Reformed theology and an emphasis on education.
missions/london-missionary-society/disag: Anglican evangelicals withdrew to found the CMS in 1799 because the LMS was not church-based; later the two clashed over comity in Madagascar, where CMS missionaries worked from 1864 until withdrawing in 1874.

When Wesleyan missionaries entered Samoa in 1835, the LMS objected that the islands were its field; the British Wesleyans agreed to withdraw, but Samoan Methodists continued and Tongan Methodists later resumed the work, leaving lasting rivalry.
missions/london-missionary-society/devia: Founded as a non-denominational society, the LMS became in practice a Congregationalist body, contrary to its Fundamental Principle.
The Fundamental Principle promised converts freedom to choose their church order, but missionaries often imposed Congregational structures and English moral codes.
Missionaries such as Pritchard in Tahiti and Helm in Matabeleland took political roles that compromised the society's claim to be above politics.
